en: Salutations to the illustrious Great Preceptor of the Upaniṣads.
The second daily lesson.
[Nyāya-pañjikā-śabdartha, 20] Now, the very distinction between human and non-human [utterances] is untenable,
because every sentence, being a sentence, possesses the presence of such indicative marks as "being a sentence" (vākyatva) and so forth— [therefore,] the Vedas were composed by an omniscient being.
Because it possesses the nature of the Veda— since such a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is possible [in the case of non-Vedic texts]— [we cite]:
"From the makers of mantras," and "Verily, this Rigveda is the breath of this great Being," and "The Ṛks and Sāmans were born."
This is because of scriptural passages such as, "From him the *chandases* were born;
from him the *yajus* was born," and because of traditional texts (*smṛti*) such as, "In each *manvantara*, this scripture is ordained differently."

Because of the application of specific designations such as *Kāṭhaka* and *Kālāpaka*, which are established by the Pāṇinian rule "adhikṛtya kṛte granthe" (when a work is composed concerning [a person], it takes his name);
because of the observation of occasional specific discourses;
and because of the non-eternal nature of such associations.
If it is argued that this is because [the sound] would fail to persist in the moments prior to and subsequent to that [manifestation],
since a sound, being a quality of the element (bhūtaguṇa), is perishable;
That is not so,
because there is no subverting argument against the inference of its being a sentence in the case of the counter-example;
otherwise, it would follow that an effect could arise without a cause.
If this is argued, it is not so;
for it is precisely "being an effect" that is being established as the probandum,
and we accept the mere absence of causality as the consequence being drawn.

If it is asked, "How can there be the status of a word (*padatva*) or a sentence (*vākyatva*) for phonemes that are not being uttered in a specific sequence?", we say no; for this status is established even when they are uttered by those who are not the original composers, just as in the case of reciting the compositions of others.
If it is further asked, "How could the first utterance occur in the absence of a composer?", we say no.
Because the very existence of a beginning is unestablished;
for, in accordance with what is observed, it is more appropriate to accept that there has always been dependent pronunciation (paratantra-uccāraṇa) just as there is today,

and thus, even though there is dependence on a person who pronounces it at all times, its beginninglessness is established through the following of the manner in which it was previously learned by each preceding generation.

If it is argued that, in the case of being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), even if there is the capacity to produce cognition—like letters carved by a woodworm—the Veda would lack the status of having meaning as its primary object because it is devoid of intentionality, we say no; for when an object is understood and remains uncontradicted, the very capacity to produce cognition constitutes the nature of *tātparya* (purport).
Furthermore, qualities such as primacy are established through the very nature of the verbal suffixes and so forth, just as in ordinary worldly sentences.
Furthermore, in our own preferred position—the *Seśvara-mīmāṃsā*—the intention of an eternal Lord is possible;

for He Himself has said: "The Śruti and the Smṛti are my very command. Likewise, the Bhāṣya states: "The Supreme Being eternally enjoins [the world] by means of the Śruti itself, which is the scripture that makes His own teaching known."
Even though that command is eternal,
the Gītā and other texts proceed as instructions on the meaning of the Śruti;
however, the Śruti itself is the primary authority for that.
And memory as well [is authoritative] because it conforms to that [perception].

If it is argued that—given its lack of a known author—there might be a suspicion of invalidity due to the absence of certainty regarding an authoritative author, as is the case with the speech of Gandharvas and the like, we say no;
for such a suspicion is removed simply by the certainty that there is an absence of defects.

If it is asked, "In the face of the suspicion that [the Veda] was composed by an unreliable author, how can there be certainty regarding the absence of defects?"— we say no, because the suspicion of an unreliable author is uprooted precisely by the acceptance [of the Veda] by the great multitude (mahājana). Why should this not be the case, just as with the acceptance of non-Buddhist scriptures?

If this is argued, we say no; for it is not the mere fact of being accepted by many people that is intended by the term "acceptance by great persons," but rather a specific kind of acceptance that is intended.
What, then, is the distinction between these two?
If this is argued, we say no, because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a visible motive.
Their acceptance [of the practice] is due to those who have no other recourse, who are seekers of their own pleasure, who desire an easy livelihood, or who are deceived by trickery;
but here it is not so.
Because the opposite of that is well-established. Thus.

Furthermore, regarding the counter-argument concerning external scriptures (*bāhyāgamapratibandha*), is this stated by the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that the authority of a scripture is based upon the authority of its author?
Or is it stated by those who accept the authority of the scriptures of the Buddhists and others?
Or rather, is it stated by the Lokāyatikas, who have discarded all scriptures concerning the world beyond?

The first [position] is not tenable; for even if the Veda were composed by Īśvara, it would be impossible to distinguish it from the non-Vedic scriptures (bāhyāgama) of the present day without such a specific act of acceptance (parigraha).
This is because the conceit that [other texts] were authored by an omniscient being, as well as the method of inferring such authorship, is unavoidable in all cases.
Not the second [alternative],
because it would follow that even one's own scripture (*svāgama*), whose authority has been accepted, would be subject to the same consequence;
and because the correspondence with perceived results can be established otherwise than through non-contradiction, as this applies equally everywhere.
Because the unconditional acceptance [of truth] that we have stated is difficult to maintain within your own system;

for this very reason, the third alternative is not tenable, since the validity of cognition in general, the validity of indirect cognition, and the validity of verbal testimony have been established, and thus validity is indeed the rule (*autsargika*) in the case of Vedic statements.

Since validity is established, and since the suspicion that the author is untrustworthy has been uprooted by the fact that the work has been accepted by an infinite number of discerning persons who are free from any limiting conditions, no suspicion of defects in the speaker can arise;
furthermore, in the case of the word, no defect such as a cataract or the like is observed, which would be inherent [in the cognition].
Even in the absence of being composed by a trustworthy author, its inherent validity remains unrefuted.

Nyāyapañcāśikā, Chapter 22: For this very reason, discerning persons proceed without hesitation toward those actions enjoined by scripture—even though they are accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort—and they desist from those prohibited, even if they are more pleasant, just as one avoids eating food mixed with poison.
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the activity of the great multitude regarding matters pertaining to the next world is fruitful.
Because it is an activity of a discerning person,
like the activity of agriculture and so forth;
for it cannot be doubted that countless discerning persons would perform an action without deception if it were fruitless.

If it is argued that this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by virtue of seeing [the world] as having suffering as its nature, we say no; for this is a refutation of what was not intended,
since what is sought to be proven (*siṣādhayiṣitatva*) is the culmination in a human goal that exceeds the suffering inherent in worldly activity.
If it is argued that they are nevertheless meaningful solely for the sake of visible purposes such as gain, honor, and fame,
that too is incorrect,
because we observe them engaging in those activities without aiming for such ends.
Furthermore, because they act with that as their objective, they are censured by the scriptures and by those devoted to them as being hypocritical.
And those who act with that as their objective obtain fame and so forth only by imitating those who have actually acted without such an objective.

Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that fame, gain, honor, and so forth would be without cause; for no one, thinking "this person has done something for me," bestows wealth and other goods acquired through great hardship, nor does anyone offer them worship.

Or rather, one praises by ascribing qualities [to something]; however, this is done only by considering that the practice of excellence has been established through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even [qualities] such as being rooted in the capacity for equanimity (*samarasa*) or being born from the attainment [of a state], ultimately originate from excellent activity rooted in treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*) and the like.
Therefore, those who act according to the established norms honor them with gifts, respect, and so forth, engaging in such conduct solely with the view that it will be seen by others.
Giving and other such acts are performed merely for the sake of pleasing people; for people feel affection for one who gives and honors them.
If it is argued that this is because of the well-known saying, "Prosperity arises from the affection of the people," we say no;

for even when those such as ascetics, the dull-witted, the blind, the deaf, the wretched, and the helpless— who are unworthy of reciprocal favors— have been gratified with gifts and honors, there is still no occurrence of the visible prosperity that would have that [affection] as its source.
For this very reason, the establishment of the distribution of wealth and other matters is entrusted precisely to ministers of policy and humor.
If you argue that people worship those [images] because they have been deceived by priests skilled in deception,
do they not deceive even themselves?
How can those who, being averse to all enjoyments, afflict themselves throughout their entire lives,
and by whom all people of sharp intellect have been deceived, be identified as deceivers by you, who possess supramundane wisdom?
If it is argued that this stream of practice is like a succession of the blind, we say no;

for the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their essential nature, their results, and their non-sublation are all directly perceived. Furthermore, by your own admission, the unconditioned acceptance [of these practices] is established as being motivated solely by the conviction that they constitute *dharma*. In this beginningless and endless tradition rooted in the *Āgama*, while the stream of practice flows on, the instigation of counterfeit versions by deceivers—whether ancient lords or recent ones—by resorting to alternative procedures, is established by both *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
And this [explanation] is logical; such is the general direction [of the argument].

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, verse 23: Counter-arguments against the inferences for the non-eternality of the Vedas— The preceding and succeeding kalpas possessed the recitation of this same Vedic compilation,
because they are kalpas, like the present kalpa.
The transmission of the Veda by the Lord is such that its ancient textual arrangement remains unaltered,
because it consists in the transmission of the Veda by a trustworthy author, just like the transmission of the Veda by a skilled contemporary teacher.
Nor is there a lack of proof regarding the basis [of the Veda] and so forth;
for even one who maintains that it possesses authority despite being of human origin establishes that very basis from that same source.

And even for one who maintains its lack of authority, authority is established precisely through the fact that its acceptance by the great multitude of people would otherwise be inexplicable, and the basis is proven from that very point.

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) regarding the composition of the Veda due to the recitation of the Sārasvata [Veda], because its tradition is likewise beginningless— just like the production of the various Vedic branches (śākhās)—
and because it is devoid of any confusion in the nature of the sentences of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas.

Thus, because there is an absence of any subverting evidence (bādhaka) against such a counter-example (vipakṣa), even the purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin) is refuted; furthermore, it has been generally criticized in the "Chapter on Inference" (Anumānādhyāya). Moreover, even in your own view, that [inference] would be an uncommon [inconclusive reason] (asādhāraṇa), since there exist similar instances (sapakṣa) such as Ayurveda and so forth.
For you do not accept that "Vedahood"—characterized by being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) and so forth—is excluded from those [other utterances].

If, merely on the basis of being objects of the application of the word "Veda," even those were made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), then there would be similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as the conventional transactions regarding the various incarnations of Īśvara, whose form is assumed according to his own will, which are distinct from the Vedas. And yet, even you do not admit these.
Or they are accepted as the Veda;
for portions spoken by the Blessed One in the *Gītā* and other works, as well as the *Śrī-Viṣṇusmṛti* and so forth, are not admitted to be the Veda.
Indeed, the *Viṣṇusmṛti* and similar texts are well known precisely as *Dharmaśāstra*.
The Vedas have no author,
because they are the Vedas; for whatever has an author, [is not a Veda].
The counter-reason— "this is not the Veda"— is thus established;
furthermore, you should not recall here the objection regarding the unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) and so forth.
If it is argued that how could a composition (*sandarbha*) be without an author, we say no;
for by the word "composition" one merely grasps a specific restriction regarding the sequence of phonemes,
and that is established even by its proceeding exactly as before, according to the principle stated previously.

Let it not be that [the scripture] lacks a logical reason; rather, let there be a positive reason: the scripture composed by the Omniscient One is authoritative, because, while being a valid means of knowledge, it is a discourse concerning supramundane matters.
If it is argued that this is like the statement, "Never indeed was I not," we say no,
because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to statements by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* and others concerning the meaning of the Vedas, or even by our own contemporary statements.
If it is argued that we shall qualify [the reason] by adding "provided there is extreme authorship," we say no;
for even so, since the fact of being composed by him would be established merely by his fashioning it exactly as it was before, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
For indeed, the Lord creates the entire universe exactly as it was before.
As we study: "The Creator fashioned the sun and moon as before.
If it is argued that, by parity of reasoning, it follows that the world must likewise be without a creator just like the Veda, we say no;
for in the case of the creation of jars and other objects as they were before, the agency of the potter, the weaver, and so forth, is established. Alas!
If it is argued that the Veda must be thus [eternal], then indeed it may be so;
for we do not claim that the present collection of the Veda is merely a collection of individual phonemes belonging to a different cosmic cycle (kalpa).
Rather, it is merely the possession of such a sequence;
the statement regarding a person's autonomy concerns the postulation of any desired order in all sentences,
and not the recitation exactly as it was previously uttered.
Thus it is well known even in the case of poetry and other such works.
If you were to prove that [the Veda] was not composed as it was in the past, then with what fault in its composition as it was in the past would you observe such a qualification?

Furthermore, the impossibility of violating the sequence in mantras and the like holds even in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), precisely because that power does not depart; or, even if it were so, because that power does not depart even when the recitation is performed as before; otherwise, there would be the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Thus it is said.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, p. 24: Even so, since creation and dissolution are possible, it might be argued that upon the interruption of the tradition and the consequent destruction of all the Vedas, God would be their creator at a later time.

This is not the case; for even then, it is more appropriate for Him—who has direct perception of the ancient Vedas—to merely set them into motion again, rather than postulating another Veda of the same kind, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) despite His power.
Furthermore, since we observe that even among those who possess power (śakti), such as ourselves, there is a reliance on what has already been established;
and since these very mantras do not lose their status as mantras even in another aeon (kalpa);
and thus, given the permanence of the mantras, it is difficult to deny the permanence of the Brāhmaṇas as well, by virtue of the same underlying principle.
Or rather, because its eternity is established by means of that very example;
for it has been stated even in the *Sārasvata-pāṭha* and other texts that there is no difference in the essential nature of the mantras and so forth:
"She who ordains Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed delivers the Vedas to him..."

"By means of eternal speech, diverse in form," "The ancients spoke this word to their predecessors," "To the unborn ones who were performing austerity, the Veda indeed manifested itself; they became seers (ṛṣis); that is the seerhood of the seers," "For this speech, without beginning or end, was emitted by the Self-existent One," "Having arranged the eternal Veda"—from such passages, it is established that even for the Lord, there is merely the promulgation of the Veda, just as for one who is not a lord.
And from what [source] is the establishment of creation and dissolution [known]?
The continuum of the universe is ultimately cut off,
because it is a continuum.
Like a series of lamps,
this continuum of the universe is initiated by inherent causes that are devoid of a continuum of visible objects,
because it is a continuum.
Like the continuity of the fire from the *araṇi* wood,
the atoms of the present world-system are preceded by another homogeneous continuum previously produced, because, while being eternal, they are the initiators of that [present system].
Like the atoms of a lamp,
even mountains will be reduced to dust, because they possess constituent parts, just like a jar.
Even the oceans will undergo desiccation because they are reservoirs of water, like small ponds; such is the inference [to be drawn].
If this is argued, we say no:

in the view that some are subject to eternal saṃsāra, there is partial sublation (*bādha*) of the first reason by those scriptures that establish such a state; and if they are excluded from the scope of the argument, the reason becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, [the argument] is rendered inconclusive (anaikāntika) by various entities such as the eternal form of the Lord and His eternal manifestations, which are established by hundreds of scriptural passages and reside within the eternal glory.
Nor can these be included within the subject of the proposition (pakṣīkāra), because that would result in either a contradiction (bādhā) or a lack of proof (asiddhi).
And the counter-arguments are as follows: the time prior to and subsequent to the number of two parārdhas established through specific calculations and so forth is not devoid of the world,
because it is time, like the present time.
These and other such [arguments] are to be inferred by oneself.

In the *Nyāyabindu-pañjikā*, [it is stated]: "No subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is clearly seen against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). And as for the claim that their strength lies in being supported by scripture (*āgama*), that is merely dependent upon the authority of scripture."
Thus, the establishment of dissolution and so forth occurs through scripture alone;
consequently, the eternity of scripture is established by scripture itself.
And it has been stated in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "The suspicion that the Veda is of human origin is not stilled by the Veda itself."
"Arising from one reason and being refuted by another reason."
Thus,

the manner in which the Vedas were received at the beginning of creation has been established as follows: "If it is argued that 'because there were no people engaged in worldly activity at the start of creation, and because the derivation of the meaning of words would be impossible,
the meaning of the Veda could not be understood by him,' that is not so."
Indeed, many [words] arise as linguistic conventions for meaning,
such as *mukta* and others, because they assume multiple forms according to the speaker's intention.
Through the persistence of the impressions of primordial consciousness,
all knowledge of the meanings of words arises for this Creator, like one who has just awakened from sleep.
They have no dwelling in a womb, nor do they undergo stages of life and so forth;
they are created as perfected in all knowledge—such is the understanding of the Veda.
Indeed, the understanding that "the Lord, having created Brahmā, gave the Vedas to him" does not arise from the scriptural passage, "He [created] Brahmā."

"The imparting of the Veda becomes meaningful only for one who knows the meaning of words; otherwise, it would be useless. Thus, by the logic of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), there must be a knower of the meaning of words."
Thus it is said.

Nyāyapañcāśikā, Śataka 26: Even the statements regarding the authorship of the Sūtras and Mantras, and [the Buddha's] birth and so forth, are accounted for solely by his being the first seer, the rememberer, and the one who initiated the tradition.
This too is established in accordance with scripture (āgama), for it is heard in the Veda: "He, the Self-Existent, brought down [the knowledge]."
Furthermore, by the command of Prajāpati, the great seers (maharṣis) perceive portions of the Vedas that they have not studied, for their majesty has been infused [by him].
And his command exists because such activities as the mental recollection of those [portions] as belonging to specific seers is useful for ritual performance.
Since the lineage of these seers is also beginningless, there is no fault such as the connection with something non-eternal.

Regarding the statement, “Whatever Manu said,” and so forth, the opponents have asserted that this refers to the beginninglessness of the tradition (*pravāhānāditva*); however, this applies equally to other narratives and the like.
And it was stated by the venerable Vyāsa: “The great seers [recovered] the Vedas, along with the Itihāsas, which had disappeared at the end of the eon.”
In former times, they attained [their goals] through austerity, having been authorized by the Self-Existent One.”
Thus [it is said].
"History" (*itihāsa*) here refers to various such accounts.

And it has been stated by that very same author in the *Dharmaśāstra*: "They say that the root of Dharma is the Veda—an unauthored mass of texts—and the tradition (*smṛti*), conduct (*śīla*), and the practice of the virtuous (*sādhvācāra*) which is pleasing to the mind for those who know it."
Thus,

the "bringing forth of branches" (*śākhāpraṇayana*) refers to the extraction of a single portion from the tree of the Veda due to the decline in the capacity of future persons at the end of the Dvāpara age.
By this, the [Vedic] designation (*samākhyā*) is fully accounted for.
Because it is the subject matter of the sacred teaching.

And all of this has been established in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "Whatever powers are heard of in the mass of the Vedas regarding the seers and others, beings of exactly such [powers] are created by the Self-born One upon seeing the Vedas."
Therefore, because they appeared even without having studied the Vedas, the eternity of the Veda is established prior to those [sages],
owing to their being the manifestors of the Vedas.
Through the refinement of asceticism (tapas), the possibility of [the Vedas] being well-spoken and so forth arises;
for by the power of austerity and the refinement resulting from the vision of the Ṛṣis, the mantras [attain their excellence].
A certain capacity is imparted [to the word] by our study, just as [the capacity for] making the meaning understood belongs to a word through its own inherent power, like any other word.
From the sight of the seer, another [person] studies; furthermore, there arises a different capacity [in him].
Therefore, this [sight] would assist in the accomplishment of a new effect.

"Or rather, this very [fact of being taught by Kaṭha and others] is the basis for the designation *Kāṭhaka* and so forth; or else, it is the excellence of the teaching [itself]. Thus, the eternity of the Veda is established."
Thus [it is said].
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, sūtra 27: The impermanence of phonemes or the impermanence of their sequence does not contradict the intended permanence of the Veda.
Nor is the permanence of phonemes a reason for the permanence of the Veda, since that would apply equally to poetry and other such works.
Furthermore, we do not accept that the section concerning sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*) is intended merely to refute the impermanence of phonemes.
And in the *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra], in the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*), it says: "If it be argued that [the world] is from sound, no;
because [the world] originates from Him, according to both perception and inference."
And for this very reason, there is permanence;
and because names and forms are the same,
there is no contradiction even in the case of repetition, as is seen from scripture.
All of this is established by the sūtras beginning with "And because of memory" (smṛteśca).

In the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*, however, [Rāmānuja] states: "If the Vedas are authoritative, then all the unprecedented (*apūrva*) categories of meaning contained within the injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras (*mantra*) inform us exactly as they exist.

Furthermore, the authority of the Vedas is established by the statement: 'The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate' (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5). Thus, having begun by establishing the correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) even for the mantras and explanatory passages, he proceeds.

The non-conventional nature of the power of words has been clearly demonstrated, as well as the distinction between verbal testimony and inference, and the classification into human and non-human origins,
and so forth. For instance, just as the possession of powers such as heat by fire, water, and the like is inherent;
Just as the capacity of the sense organs, such as the eye and others, to produce cognition is inherent,
so too the capacity of a word to convey meaning is inherent.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that a word’s power to convey meaning is rooted in convention, as is the case with hand gestures and the like.
Even when there is no interruption in the continuity of hearing and so forth, [the connection] is not understood due to ignorance of the person who established the convention;
all those things which are rooted in convention are known either directly or through a lineage of transmission.
Nor is it proper to conceive [the relationship] as being like the word "Devadatta" and so forth; for in those cases, a convention is known either directly or through tradition.
But in the case of words such as "cow," even though the continuity of usage is beginningless, their power to convey meaning is inherent, precisely because no convention is known.

Just as fire and other elements possess the power of heat and so forth, and the sense organs possess the power of cognition, the word also must necessarily be admitted to possess the power of conveying meaning.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, Section 29: Now, if it is argued that, like the sense organs, the capacity of a word to convey meaning is innate, why does it require the apprehension of a relationship for that purpose?
It is replied: "Like a logical mark (liṅga)."

Just as smoke and the like, when their relation to fire and so forth is known to be invariant, generate the cognition of fire and so forth, so too the word, when its relation to a specific object is known to be invariant, generates the cognition of that specific object. If this is the case, then the word would also be a logical mark (liṅga) of the specific object, and thus it would be nothing but inference.
It is not so;
the relationship between word and meaning is precisely that of the signified and the signifier,
whereas the relationship of smoke and the like is of a different kind.
The distinction is that it produces cognition by way of making known that relationship.

Thus, since it is observed that [the word] possesses the capacity to convey meaning for one who has grasped the relationship, it is determined that even when the beginningless continuity of connection is uninterrupted, the very capacity to convey meaning due to the lack of knowledge of the convention is indeed *śakti* (inherent power).

Thus, those collections of words which consist of groups of expressive terms and are designated by the term "sentence" (*vākya*) because they convey a specific relation [of meaning], are called "human" (*pauruṣeya*) when their sequence of utterance is preceded by human intention.
However, where the sequence of utterance is always preceded by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by preceding sequences of utterance, [they are not human].
It is said that those Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
This very thing constitutes both the non-human origin and the eternity of the Vedas:
namely, that they are to be uttered in that very same sequence by recollecting the specific sequence through the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous utterance of that sequence.
Through that specific sequence, those very collections of syllables, established as the Vedas, exist with infinite branches, divided into the distinctions of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan.
In this context, the omission of the Atharva Veda by Aṅgiras was intended to indicate its inclusion within the [other] Vedas.
Likewise, even regarding the designation of "the three Vedas," one must understand that there is a difference in intention.
Furthermore, all of this is threefold in form, consisting of mantras, arthavādas, and so forth.
In this context, "mantra" refers to that which is the object of the linguistic usage of authoritative persons;
and it assists by means of illuminating the meaning of what is to be performed and so forth.
Nor is this alone its defining characteristic.
Because [the definition] does not extend to such cases as "For the spring," and so forth;
for even mantras such as "They sacrifice kapiñjala birds to the spring" have been analyzed by the Mīmāṃsakas as being primarily injunctive (vidhi).

Indeed, that mantra is divided into various types, such as those that describe an action currently being performed (kriyamāṇānuvādī), hymns of praise (stotra), recitations (śastra), and silent prayers (japya).

Regarding the efficacy of mantras in various languages such as Paiśāca and Māgadha, the cause lies in their specific seed-syllables (*bīja*), phonetic classes, and so forth. Merely bearing the name of a deity worthy of faith does not obstruct the power of those syllables;
rather, such [mantras] were created by Īśvara and others for the purpose of deception, by manifesting swift and trivial results.
In the case of mantras in vernacular languages marked with the names of Garuḍa and others, however, they also serve the purpose of evoking the recollection of those respective deities.
By this, the grammatical analysis of mantras is established.
As for the seventy million great mantras (mahāmantra) which are established in the authoritative scriptures, [they are likewise included].

These [practices] are divided into Vedic and Tantric based on the application or non-application of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and other such criteria. Among these, the terminology "Tantric" is employed for the purpose of establishing the eligibility of Śūdras and others, and not because they are non-Vedic.
This is because, like the designations of the various divisions such as Śrauta and Smārta rites, there is no difference in their being established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, for all mantras, whether they function through an intermediary or directly, the Supreme Self alone is the subject to be realized and the bestower of the fruit.
Regarding those that function through an intermediary, they culminate in Brahman in many ways due to the diversity of their ritual applications (viniyoga).
Because they are the bodies of those respective deities, because they abide as their constituent parts,
and by virtue of the principle of Indra and the others, all of these reside within the Lord.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa, verse 31: An *arthavāda* is indeed a specific type of statement that reinforces activity prompted by an injunction (*vidhi*).

It is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own object when that object is not contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, because its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is never lost.
Even where there is a cognition of contradiction, its authority is established through the metaphorical attribution of a non-contradictory meaning;
and it has been settled in such sections as the *Arthavāda-adhikaraṇa* that this [authority] sometimes becomes valid by forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction (*vidhi*).
However, that which has as its object a specific matter that is an end in itself attains validity even through its independence; this is established by the *Samanvaya-sūtra*.
When there is a desire to attain that [end], there arises the operation of sentences concerning the means thereto.
And that [operation] is fourfold, distinguished as censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), "deeds of others" (*parakṛti*), and "ancient accounts" (*purākalpa*).
In this context, "censure" (nindā) is a statement regarding the defects of that which is to be prohibited, etc., serving as a supplement to a prohibition;
"praise" (praśaṃsā) is a statement regarding the qualities of that which is to be enjoined, etc., serving as a supplement to an injunction;
and "the account of another's deed" (parakṛti) is a specific narrative connected with a single [central] theme.
But the ancient tradition is followed by many.
In this context, an injunction (*vidhi*) is a statement consisting of beneficial instruction.

It is of many kinds—distinguished as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), combined (*saṃvalita*), positive injunctions (*vidhi*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), and so forth.
Restriction (*niyama*) and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) are also merely varieties of injunction.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding what has not yet been obtained, there is the attainment [of that object]; in the case of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is the completion of what has already been partially obtained; whereas in the case of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is the sublation (*bādha*) of what is already obtained in one respect.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdakhaṇḍa 33: Now, what indeed is the meaning of the suffixes such as *liṅ* (the optative) in this context?

It cannot be the *apūrva* (unseen potency), because it is impossible to acquire linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) with respect to that which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If, however, it were within the scope of that [injunction], its status as something previously unknown (*apūrva*) would be contradicted;
furthermore, if the learner's proficiency were brought about by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that its establishment occurs through deliberation (*vimarśa*), we say no.

Because deliberation (*vimarśa*) is not admitted to be something distinct from memory and experience; because even for that which is etymologically derived from "action" (*kriyā*) and "effect" (*kārya*), it must be sustained by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth despite its lack of syntactic fitness (*anvayāyogyatā*); and because it is impossible to alter the primary denotation (*abhidhāna*).
Furthermore, there is no rule that initial linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) must occur only with respect to something to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Likewise, immediately upon hearing the words of an elderly person who prompts action, such as "Bring the cow," an observer standing nearby who seeks to acquire linguistic knowledge perceives a person engaged in bringing the cow; because the activity of a conscious being is preceded by the cognition of it as something to be accomplished, and because the elderly person being prompted possesses the cognition of it as something to be accomplished.

Since no other cause is observed, one concludes that "the statement of the experienced elder, namely 'that which is seen immediately after something else is its cause,' is indeed the cause of the learner's cognition of the causal relationship.
Similarly, when someone says to another, "A son has been born to you," it is understood that the birth of a son is known to be a source of joy for him.

One who seeks to understand, upon observing the expansion of the face of a person who has heard the news of a son’s birth, infers that this is caused by the cognition of a pleasant object; and since no other cause for that cognition is perceived, he concludes that the sentence announcing the son’s birth itself is the cause.
Nor should it be argued that the pleasantness of the son’s birth was unknown to the child.

Logicians maintain that since it is possible for such a thing to occur even during the initial stage of learning a second language— as is the case with one whose son was born after he had already attained maturity— an example [of a person who learns a language from birth] need not be strictly adhered to as a definitive illustration.

Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdapariccheda, 34: And therefore, what is not plausible? That a child desiring to learn, upon observing that a person who hears of the acquisition of those things—such as foods and edibles—which are recognized as being dear to children, exhibits a facial expansion and so forth, thereby acquires linguistic proficiency.
If it is argued that a facial expansion can also occur due to the recollection of other pleasant things, etc., [we reply:]...
In the same way, the understanding that "bringing the cow" is to be performed could also arise through the recollection of other purposes dependent upon it, such as [the speaker's] own [desire].

If it is argued that the determination [of the specific meaning] occurs due to the force of a particular proximity (*āsatti*) and because it follows from multiple usages, this is equal [to our position].

Even so, if it is argued that the distinction remains difficult to ascertain because there is the possibility of other meanings—such as causes of joy like the birth of a beloved child, an easy delivery, or sweet speech—associated with those various [other] things, we say no.

Even in the case of a sentence such as "Bring the cow," which conveys a range of duties including bringing the calf together with it and obtaining milk, how could one determine that this sentence conveys only the duty of bringing the cow, given that the act of bringing the cow is possible for those other purposes as well? If you argue that this is determined by the power of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and by the support of observed facts (*dṛṣṭānugraha*), then the same applies here.

Thus, because the reconciliation of the example regarding the statement about the birth of a son is difficult for those of dull intellect to grasp, the Commentator has set it aside and demonstrated a much clearer method of linguistic acquisition—both spontaneous and intentional.
This is now recorded here: "It is said that children thus determine the relationship between words and their meanings:

when their mother, father, and others say, 'Know this as *amba* (mother),' 'this as *tāta* (father),' 'this as *mātula* (uncle),' and so on, referring to the moon, cattle, humans, deer, birds, reptiles, and the like..."
And understand this:

with this intention, pointing repeatedly with his finger at various objects while using various words, he observed that after being trained many times, those [children] gradually produced within themselves a cognition of those very objects by means of those very words; thus, [he understood] the relationship between word and object.

Because no other relationship [between word and meaning] is observed and because the person who established the convention is unknown, they conclude that the employment of those words for those objects is based on their power to convey meaning. Furthermore, having been instructed by previous elders that "this is the meaning of this word" regarding words both familiar and unfamiliar, and having thus understood the meaning of all words, they employ them to communicate specific meanings to others.
They employ a collection of sentences.

Furthermore, it is quite possible to determine the relationship between a word and its meaning through another method: suppose a certain person is dispatched with the instruction, "Inform Devadatta that your father is doing well," using hand gestures and the like; once he has set about informing him, he employs the sentence, "Your father is doing well."

Another person standing nearby, desiring to learn and like a mute, observes specific gestures; having understood that the speaker is engaged in making something known and has followed him, and having heard this word employed for the purpose of making that thing known, he determines:
"This word is the cause of the cognition of that object. Thus, the insistence that linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) occurs only through the understanding of a causal relationship is groundless.
In the *Nyāyapariśiṣṭa* (Śa 35), in place of the sentence "Your father is well," another example—"A staff is standing in the room"—is merely cited elsewhere.
Therefore, the primary acquisition of linguistic meaning (*vyutpatti*) is established even regarding what is unaccomplished (*asiddha*).
Or, let it be that the primary acquisition of meaning occurs only with respect to the effect (*kārya*).
Nevertheless, the power of words must be discerned solely through the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of their usage;
for words are employed by those who have no intention of enjoining an action, as in the following:
"Who is that king? The Kaurava."
For in this case, the question arises merely out of curiosity,

and the answer likewise conforms to that. Therefore, just as the individual power of words is extracted according to possibility— whether with respect to an accomplished entity (*siddha*) or an action to be performed (*kārya*)— so it is here.

Likewise, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is also [determined] accordingly; for even though the capacity to serve as a means of linguistic derivation belongs [to the word], it is logical that the object of the intention of all words is the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished).
Furthermore, even in a sentence expressing a *kārya*, the predominance of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), characterized by its being the motivator (*pravartaka*) and so forth, must be sought.

Because it is impossible for anything other than pleasure and the absence of pain to be, by its own nature, an incentive toward itself, and because even at the stage of learning, actions such as bringing [something] are understood to be incentives for activity only as being subordinate to something else— namely, pleasure or the cessation of pain—
it follows that the cognition of being an end-in-itself (*kāryatva*) applies directly only to pleasure or the cessation of pain.
Since it serves that purpose, when one undertakes the means to achieve it,

the understanding of its being an effect (kāryatā) is established even in the case of the means-to-the-means, because it is required just like the primary means. Furthermore, the apūrva is not of the nature of pleasure and so forth.
Nor is it accepted that [the Vedic injunction] prompts action by being the means to that [pleasure];

for even if such acceptance were granted, it would be impossible to postulate that either the form of the deity's pleasure itself—or the pleasure of the deity as established by the Śruti and other sources—is what is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as the cause of the attainment of a result occurring at a later time, just like the pleasure of a worldly object of service;
this is also because of the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice and others.

Just as the specific location of installation, the hundredfold torments [of hell], or the employment of ghee, collyrium, goats, and so forth, are required by the injunction and are well-known, let the *apūrva*—consisting essentially of the propitiation of the deity—be postulated either as the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) or as its instrumental medium; what need is there for anything else?

And as for what those who are half-Lokāyatikas say: "The gods possess no physical body, no receiving of oblations, no simultaneous presence at rituals, no feeling of affection, and no bestowing of fruits. (Nyāyapariśiṣṭa, Śabdanirūpaṇa, verse 36)
Thus, that [objection] as well is based on a lack of understanding of Jaimini’s true intention;

for it is not proper to discard the forms of deities and so forth—which are established by the Veda, which is inherently authoritative, as well as by Smṛti and Purāṇas, and which lie beyond the scope of any subverting or corroborating means of knowledge.
Nor can sublation be suspected merely because of non-perception among those who are incapable [of perceiving them].
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle, and because it would result in the doctrine of the Lokāyatas being directly asserted;

for even in explanatory passages (arthavādas) that serve as supplements to injunctions, there is no fault such as "splitting the sentence" (vākyabheda), since they express their own literal meaning precisely for the sake of that [injunction].
Even when [the texts] are intent upon praise and so forth, there is no sublation of the primary meaning,
because there is no sublation of their own referent, and it is impossible to abandon their own referent;
nor is all praise unreal.
Nor is praise established by mentioning a quality that does not exist;
however, where there is a sublation of the primary meaning,
even there some figurative basis is intended.
Otherwise, it would be a mere mockery;
nor would it be a mere form of persuasion,
because such knowledge does not assist a person's engagement [in action].
Furthermore, it is impossible for the one who ascertains [the meaning] to be ignorant of that [meaning],
otherwise it would follow that his activity is rooted in delusion;
and according to the method of the *Samanvaya* section, there are portions [of the text] whose sole purpose is to establish what is already established.
Following upon that are the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth.

[Objection: But in the section on *arthavādas* (Nyāyasudhā, Pāda 1, Adhikaraṇa 2), it was stated that "because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, the *arthavādas* serve the purpose of praising the injunctions"—thus, the status of all *arthavādas* as being in syntactical unity with injunctions was established.
However, in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, how can there be a statement that contradicts this? [Response:

Not so. In the section on *arthavādas*, it was established merely to the extent that validity is possible through syntactical unity with injunctions, in order to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that *arthavādas* lack authority.

As for the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that, if [the Upaniṣads] were syntactically unified with injunctions, they would lack the purport of revealing the nature of Brahman— this is refuted in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* by establishing that even sentences whose subjects are matters that are inherently purposeful in themselves, such as the existence of a treasure in a room, possess validity through syntactical independence; thus, there is no contradiction.

Moreover, it is observed even in grammar and other sciences that contradictions are resolved through the systematic allocation of subject matter (*viṣayavyavasthā*) among sentences that express various meanings, both general (*autsargika*) and exceptional (*āpavādika*).
For this very reason, the Vedic statement that "the *arthavādas* are supplements to the *brāhmaṇas*" should be understood as referring to the general domain.

As for the ingenious theory of the followers of Kumārila—that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is precisely the "efficient force of the word" (*śabdabhāvanā*)—[it is set aside by this principle].
But that [position] is refuted by the contradiction with actual experience;
for a person hearing an injunctive sentence does not perceive that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth denote their own operation.
Therefore, one thinks, "I must act.

Yet, even if the nature of the sacrifice and the like, along with the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, were presented together by some sentence, no one is ever observed to actually act.

Furthermore, if the optative suffix and the like were the instigator of action merely through their operation characterized as being known, or through their operation characterized as a causal power (*śakti*), it would follow that activity would occur even before the acquisition of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Even if linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) were a cooperative cause [for the understanding of the optative suffix], its object must be stated, because it is impossible for that convention to be objectless while depending on such a [suffix].
Furthermore, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others are nowhere conventionally established as having their own operation (*svavyāpāra*) as their object;
for all words are indeed conventionally established only with respect to objects other than their own operation.

Furthermore, those words such as "denotation" (*abhidhā*) and so forth do not denote their own function by way of specific designation (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*); rather, because they operate upon the function of wordhood in general, their own function is also included by being subsumed under the common attribute (*sāmānyopādhi*).

For this very reason, since the denotatum of words such as "denotation" (abhidhā) and their cause are understood in a general sense, the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (vyutpatti) is possible. However, in the case of the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth, proficiency would have to arise once its own operation is perceived; and if that perception [of the operation] were by one who already possesses proficiency, [it would lead to a circularity].
There would be mutual dependence; and if it were by one who is untrained, there would be an over-extension of the principle. Thus.

The meaning conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and similar affixes is not merely the status of being a means to what is desired, because we observe their simultaneous usage in such expressions as: "This is a means to what you desire; therefore, do it."

Nor is this a case of tautology based on respect and so forth, because the comprehension is not of that nature, and because it is impossible to indicate both the reason and the probandum [simultaneously].
If it is argued that [the injunction] is also seen in the form "this must be done; therefore, do this," we say no.
This is because there is no contradiction in intending to express a general and a specific meaning— as in the statement, "This is the duty of a Brahmin; therefore, it must also be performed by you"—
whereas if one intends to express only an absolutely identical meaning, then even in that case, such usage would be improper.
For this very reason, it is refuted that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is merely the desire of a trustworthy speaker;
for [the meaning is] "this is desired by the trustworthy one."
This is because we observe specific intentions in the speaker who acts with the thought, "This is my duty.

Nor should it be argued that, simply because it is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), an injunction (*vidhi*)—like an invitation (*nimantraṇā*) and so forth—is merely the intention of the speaker; for this would lead to inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to [other meanings] such as possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and those specifically prescribed [by grammarians].

If unity were established merely by being denotable by a single word, then even the illustrative example would fail to be proven, given the consequence that words with multiple meanings would collapse.
Although Udayana’s argument regarding the impossibility of negation applies to the opponent's view, it does not touch upon our own position.

If the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) is "to be performed" (*kartavyatā*), there is no contradiction in its connection with the negative particle *nañ* in the expression "it is not to be performed" (*na kartavyaḥ*).
Furthermore, "to be performed" consists precisely in being achievable through the agent's activity.

Thus, in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*, following the question, "What is this meaning accepted for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth? it was replied: "The root *yaji* [is used] in the sense of 'worship of the gods'..."

Thus, there is nothing inconsistent in the view that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express the fact that the meaning of the verbal root— such as sacrifice, which consists in the propitiation of a deity— is to be accomplished by the agent’s activity, as this is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*);
for what must be expressed by suffixes denoting an agent is the manner in which the meaning of the verbal root is related to the agent’s activity,
while others say it is [the expression of] its pastness, presentness, and so forth.
"But the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth express that which is to be accomplished by the agent’s activity.

And in the Bhāṣya on the first sūtra: "Therefore, even in injunctive sentences, it is determined that what is expressed by the optative suffix and the like is merely the fact that the meaning of the verbal root is to be accomplished by the agent’s activity—a fact already established by the science of grammar; and furthermore, that the meaning of the root, such as sacrifice (*yāga*), consists in the propitiation of the Supreme Person who dwells within the deities such as Agni."
"Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit [results] from the Supreme Person who has been propitiated; this will be established by the sūtra: 'The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical'.
Here, the phrase "merely being accomplished through the agent's activity" is stated to demonstrate the extracted meaning;

however, the mode of comprehension in cases such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is indeed with the agent as primary, [understood] as qualified by a sacrifice and so forth to be accomplished by one's own activity.
As it was stated in the *Dīpa* regarding the section on the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*): "One should sacrifice, one should meditate"— for here the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the agent.
"Therefore, the scripture instructs only the agent.

And it has been stated in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* as well: "In such injunctions as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' the words 'one desiring heaven' and so forth—which provide the specific identity of the agent denoted by the verbal suffix—functioning to provide the specific identity of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is not in contradiction with the science of grammar."

Although the *Dīpa* text is devoted solely to the point that the agentivity (*kartṛtva*) of the person is established by scripture (*śruti*), nevertheless, it refutes the Sāṃkhya school by demonstrating that even in the case of optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like—which primarily denote the state of being accomplished through the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—the function [of the suffix] has the agent as its primary referent. Therefore, because it serves that purpose, it should be understood as being intent on that very point there as well.

Furthermore, the skillful grammatical analyses such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) being "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) reveal that the meaning of the verbal root is construed precisely as the object of the act of doing (*kṛti*).
In the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, *Śataka* 38, this has been clarified in the *Śrī Gītābhāṣya*: "In the word ‘yudhyasva’ (‘fight’), the explanation is ‘commence the action known as battle.

[Objection: Since, according to grammar, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*), how can there be an accusative case ending for a qualifier of an action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*)?
For a qualifier does not construe with its qualificand in the sense that "one should bring about the qualifier by means of the qualificand."
Because you accept that either the fruit or the *apūrva* is what is to be brought into being (*bhāvya*);
furthermore, in cases such as present verbal designations, even though there is no other object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the mere qualifier is not the *sādhya*,
nor is a word ending in the nominative case a qualifier of the action.

Even on the view that [the suffix] denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), there would be the consequence of its non-connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because it is impossible for something unconnected to function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a verbal root ending in a non-objective case-ending and [a word] ending in an objective case-ending?"

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) even with a word ending in an instrumental case; nor is any fault observed in its connection as the object (*karman*) when it is being understood as such,

for there is no contradiction even in the sentence-meaning "one desiring heaven should perform a sacrifice," just as in the case of the sentence-meaning "one desiring priyaṅgu rice should engage in agriculture."

In that very way, since its status as a means [to the goal] is established by implication (*arthataḥ*), the expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇākāṅkṣā*)—expressed by "by what?"—is also satisfied. Furthermore, the connection of the instrumental case ending with the name does not necessarily imply grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for it is naturally construed even with the sense: "one should perform the worship of the deity by means of specific rites bearing those respective names."
Because it is possible to express [the relationship] through a non-co-referential indication by means of both general and specific forms;

otherwise, just as in the expression "one should please the king with flattery," there would be the undesirable consequence that even the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) in "perform a sacrifice" (*yāgaṃ kuru*) would be something to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
since it is impossible for that very [meaning], being of the nature of the agent's activity, to be its own object of accomplishment.
Because either the base or the suffix remains indifferent when the action is accomplished,
[one says] "one," "two," etc.
It is like [the expression] "many," and so forth.
Even there, when one intends to express the status of being an object (*karmatā*), that too is done either by intending another operation of the agent (*kartṛvyāpārāntara*), or...

Alternatively, the explanation may be carried out by means of metaphorical attribution (upacāra), as in the case of "he performs the action of fetching water" and so forth. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā).
Because conventional discourse is brought to its conclusion through non-ascension [into] dependent origination,
the application of such statements as "one performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" is favorable to our position.
Therefore, what [is there], by what [means]?
How? As stated by you; for what purpose? What?
By what?
Regarding the fourfold expectancy of "how": the expectancy of "for what purpose" is fulfilled by [the mention of] heaven and so forth;

the expectancy of "what [is it that should be done]"—namely, "one should gratify the deity"—remains unappeased; and the expectancy of "by what means" is fulfilled by the name and other factors such as "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma."
As for the fulfillment of the inquiry "how [is it accomplished]?", that is exactly the same for both you and us; such is the path of verbal testimony (*śabda*).

Therefore, from sentences such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which inform the respective qualified agent of their connection with the specific meaning of the verbal root as the objective to be achieved, it is understood from the sentence itself that the result arises from the performance of those respective root-meanings, and the transgression (*pratyavāya*) from non-performance, due to the volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the Ruler of All.

However, the specific mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) directed toward intermediate deities is a secondary consequence (*ānuṣaṅgika*) of the act of sacrificing through the mediation of those [deities], similar to the satisfaction of the person eating at a *śrāddha* feast.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the fruits of actions performed in previous *kalpas* would not arise when the hosts of deities from those former *kalpas* have dissolved during the subsequent dissolution (*pralaya*).
For this very reason, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is the command for only one [Supreme Lord].
Furthermore, just as the status of being a worshipper depends upon Him, so too does the status of being an object of worship depend upon Him.
Regarding this, the venerable Nārāyaṇārya has stated: "Some have declared that it is the injunction of the authoritative teacher who desires one's welfare;
the Blessed Commentator also agreed with this very point."
Thus [it is said].
And here, the commentary is intended as follows: "Having revealed the scripture that makes one understand its own teaching.
This is established by the force of the statement regarding punishment and favor resulting from the observance or transgression of injunctions and prohibitions:
"The Śruti and Smṛti are my very command; he who acts in transgression of it..."
"One who violates my command is a traitor to me; even if he is my devotee, he is certainly not a Vaiṣṇava."
Thus [it is said].
And it has been explained by the grammarians that "injunction (*vidhi*) is instigation (*preraṇā*)," and instigation is indeed command (*śāsana*).

And the authors of the *Tattvaratnākara* have stated as follows: "O Lord of Raṅga, the proponents of false views [hold] that either the action (*kriyā*), its power (*tacchakti*), some such unprecedented force (*apūrva*), or the grace of the ancestors and gods, bestows the fruit upon the agent."

The elders of the three Vedas maintain that even the fruit of your sacrifices and charitable works arises from your own grace, and that the various injunctions for those acts are themselves your instigation.

And among the various injunctions such as the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*), the specific intentions of the Ruler have been revealed: “O Śrīraṅgarāja, Your Sovereign! Your commands are the obligatory injunctions with their specific causes; the injunction for those desiring heaven and other rewards is Your permission (*anujñā*). The scriptural teaching on malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is the means for bringing under control the hearts of the deceitful. Indeed, every scripture that announces Your protective intent is Your eternal ordinance.”
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, the Draviḍabhāṣya is cited in the Vedārthasaṅgraha: "Knowing those who follow his own teaching, the wise one, skilled in action, [acts] out of compassion, by his very nature, and with faith.
Immediately thereafter, this same meaning is also shown in the Bhagavadgītā: "Those men who constantly practice this teaching of mine..."
Those who possess faith and do not find fault are also liberated from their karmic actions.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded regarding all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of discernment.

"Thus, having praised those who follow their own [inherent] ignorance and censured those who act otherwise, and having further stated that those who do not maintain their own knowledge fall within the category of the *āsura* nature and are destined for the lowest state— such indeed is the meaning of the word 'injunction' (*vidhi*) accepted by the Vedāntins.
Thus some others have also declared.

Therefore, since an instigation (*preṣaṇā*) without an object is impossible, it follows that either the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be accomplished by the agent’s activity— which has the injunction as its fundamental basis— or the instigation itself, extending up to that state of being accomplished, is the unique meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like. This being established, it is logical that the instigation alone— expounded as the meaning of the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) by virtue of sharing the same status as "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*) and the other terms mentioned in the rule *Pāṇini 3.3.161*, namely "the optative is used in the senses of injunction, invitation, permission, request, inquiry, and entreaty"— is what is denoted by words such as the optative suffix.
Others, however, maintain that even otherwise, the act of sending is indeed included within [the meaning of the verb].

And this fact that injunctive sentences consist of the command of the Lord was indeed indicated by Jaimini himself in the aphorism: "Dharma is a matter characterized by *codanā*. For the word *codanā* indicates a certain person who impels (*codaka*). This is made clear even from an example cited in the *Śabarabhāṣya*, though it may not strike the heart: "For it is observed [in common usage] that one says, 'I am doing this because I have been urged by my teacher. (Nyāyapañcāśikā, Chapter 3, Verse 39)
Nyāyapañjikā, Śabara-bhāṣya 40: Thus, the person indicated by the word *codanā* has already been specifically shown by his own statement.
Furthermore, in the *Autpattika-sūtra*, [Jaimini] composed the sūtra: "The knowledge of that [Dharma] is instruction (*upadeśa*).
For instruction, too, implies an instructor.

In the aphoristic fragment, “*tatpramāṇaṃ bādarāyaṇasya*,” he has indicated his own alignment of intention with Bādarāyaṇa, who was his own teacher. And that Bādarāyaṇa demonstrated to his own disciple Jaimini—whom he accepted as having realized the reality of the Lord and other principles—in many aphorisms such as “*sākṣādapyavirodhaṃ jaiminiḥ*,” that there is no contradiction [with the Upanishads]. Any occasional rejection, however, is intended either to dispel the delusion of those of dull intellect regarding the superficial meaning of statements made by others for some other purpose, or to remove even minor lapses; it is not a sign for postulating a primary contradiction.

And in the section concerning *arthavādas*, by stating "But because they form a single sentence with an injunction, they serve the purpose of praising the injunctions," [the author] indicates— through the mention of the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth that express the injunction in the form of an impulsion—

that the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), as a whole, is indicated by way of its constituent parts; and by asserting that the *arthavādas* form a single sentence with that [injunction], he suggests that the entire Veda possesses the nature of an injunction consisting of the Lord’s command, as explicitly stated in those very words.
In this same way, it should be understood in other cases as well.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa 41: Thus, scripture (śruti) is indeed the command of the Lord;
and because it conforms to that, tradition (smṛti) is also [authoritative].
For the Vedas, consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Mantras, and Arthavādas, are infinite, intermingled, scattered, and at times even lost.

In this regard, Manu and others who possess complete knowledge of the Vedas accurately record the meanings of the Vedic texts as they have personally experienced them, in order to pacify the confusion regarding the correct practice of reality among those who possess only partial knowledge in specific times and places.
Therefore, the determination of the meaning of ancient speech is rooted in them.
However, some say that when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, an option for performance arises because the Smṛti leads one to infer another source (the Śruti).

Others maintain that even though all those possessing the three qualities (*guṇatrayavat*) may be most authoritative (*āptatama*), because the possibility of occasional error exists, the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*. However, in the investigation of reality (*tattva-viṣaya*), when there is a contradiction, there is either sublation (*bādha*) or a shift in meaning (*ānyaparya*).
Because conceptual construction is impossible regarding a real entity (*vastu*),
the determination [of the object] occurs through the relative strength of the grasping [of the memory], despite the contradiction between two memories.
Furthermore, the lack of confidence in all cases does not follow from the invalidity of memories in some instances.
Because no sublation is observed,
because there is an absence of any fixed indicative mark for the postulation of defects in the cause,
and because it is logical to postulate that the Veda alone is the source— since otherwise the acceptance [of the Smṛti] would be inexplicable given the abundance of corroboration and other factors.
Otherwise, if all human speech were rendered invalid, the authority of scripture (āgama) would be lost;
nor can it be said that this is not undesirable, for we observe that people engage in learning by taking the words of trustworthy persons, such as their fathers, as authoritative.

Nor does even occasional agreement provide grounds for confidence in non-Vedic scriptures (bāhyāgama), because they frequently contradict direct perception and Vedic revelation, lack acceptance by the followers of the Vedas, are well-known as being outside the Vedic fold, and reject the Vedas themselves; thus, it is impossible to postulate a Veda as their source.
Furthermore, it is not possible for them to have as their source a perception or other means of knowledge that transcends the ordinary world.
Even the postulation that [the Smṛti] is rooted in yogic direct perception would apply only to cases not contradicted by the Veda;
nor is there certainty even in those cases,
because the possibility of contrary experience still exists.
Furthermore, the Smṛtis, which are rooted in the Veda, are of three kinds—namely, the Dharmaśāstras, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas.
Among these, the first two (the Dharmaśāstras and Itihāsas) are included within a single field of knowledge because they are not far removed [from the Veda].

In this regard, the determination of their relative strength based on the distinction between those [Smṛtis] that are authorized and those that are unauthorized has been demonstrated in the Ābhāsa-āhnika.
In the Purāṇas as well, there is a classification into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and so forth.
Nyāyapañjikā, Chapter 42: Furthermore, as for the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and Pañcarātra systems, these too are indeed specific branches of the Dharmaśāstras;
the Sāṃkhya is that scripture which is dedicated to demonstrating the yoga of knowledge consisting of the contemplation of the perfectly pure self.

The *yoga* system is the scripture whose culmination is the practice of action reaching the limit of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The *Pāśupata* system is that which teaches the worship of Paśupati as the object for those who are not yet awakened.
However, the *Pañcarātra* scripture is that which is engaged in teaching the exclusive worship of the Lord as the object for those who are awakened.
And these [scriptures] are, in certain respects, mutually dependent; however,
when there is mutual contradiction, the determination of their relative strength is made according to the Veda, while in any part that contradicts the Veda, there is sublation.
For negligence is possible among all those who are not lords, whereas deception can occur even toward the Lord himself, who is directly intent on deluding the Asuras and others;
as was said by the Blessed One himself: "O Rudra, O mighty-armed one, you indeed must cause delusive scriptures to be composed."
Having shown that it requires little effort, demonstrate the fruit quickly.
"I shall practice delusion so that I may delude the mind. Thus [he thought].
Therefore, there is the Sāṃkhya presentation of primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth as being uncontrolled by a Lord;
and in Yoga, having accepted a Lord, there is the description of His sovereignty as conceived through the reflection of Him as a mere instrumental cause;
and in Pāśupata, there is the conceptualization of a reversal of the higher and lower principles, as well as practices and so forth that contradict the Vedas.
Having set aside all of that, validity must be accepted in the remaining portion;
however, this cannot be accomplished by those of little knowledge, like the separation of husk from grain.
For this reason, there is a refutation of the [other] three in the Śārīraka.
The *Pañcarātra* is entirely authoritative, whether as scripture (*śruti*) or as tradition (*smṛti*), because it lacks contradiction with direct revelation and other authorities;

and because, in the *Mahābhārata*, even the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra*— the most trustworthy— is said to be rooted in it, and because of its special acceptance by Vyāsa and others out of great respect, and because, being rooted in the compassion of the Lord, it is free from the possibility of defects in its cause.
“Having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas as it is, the learned Lord Hari, out of compassion for his devotees, has condensed [this work] for their ease.”
And for this reason, its authority is manifest in that very context:

because it accepts the authority of the Veda; because it explains its meaning extensively; because it provides the cause for clarifying that [meaning]; because it speaks for the sake of protecting the grammatically correct words; because it has Nārada and others as listeners who are superior in their virtuous nature (*sattva*);
and because such a composition could not possibly be for the purpose of deception.
Because this would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) elsewhere as well;
for passages such as "The Vedas have been studied, O Blessed One," have as their purport merely the difficulty of grasping [the truth], and do not consist in a censure of the Vedas.
Even if they were of the nature of censure, they would function—like the censure of the *udita* fire-oblation—to praise that which is other than what is censured.

Since the fact that such passages as "The one named Saṅkarṣaṇa, the individual soul (jīva), is born" refer to incarnations and the like is established in that very [text], the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras]— having formulated the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the two sūtras "Because of the impossibility of origination" (*utpattyasaṃbhavāt*) and "And because the instrument cannot originate from the agent" (*na ca kartuḥ karaṇam*)— refuted the denial of its authority with the two sūtras "Or, if there is the state of being consciousness and so forth, there is no prohibition of that" (*vijñānādibhāve vā tadapratiṣedhaḥ*) and "And because of contradiction" (*vipratiṣedhācca*).

Likewise, the refutation of various weak doubts—such as those concerning the lack of a foundational source, the absence of acceptance of what is non-existent and the presence of acceptance of what is existent, the avoidance of Vedic purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the prescription of non-Vedic purificatory rites, the absence of an enumeration of the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and the abundance of trivial sciences (*kṣudravidyā*)—has been elaborately set forth by the venerable Yāmunamuni; therefore, it is not expanded upon here.
Nyāyapañcānanapaddhati, Chapter 43: Thus, because it is rooted directly in the compassion of the Lord, this [work] possesses superiority over the compendia of Manu and others.

Furthermore, since those [other works] are subject to the three *guṇas*, the possibility of occasional error and so forth exists; consequently, they may even be sublated when they contradict the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

For it has been stated even in the Bhāṣya, in the section beginning with "And also above that," that the authority of the Smṛtis and so forth rests solely upon their being rooted in Śruti: "In the Dharmaśāstras, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, which are rooted in the mixed Brāhmaṇas, Mantras, and Arthavādas."
From that very point, it is also indicated that their established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that these [Vedic texts] have their roots in various scattered branches (*viprakīrṇa-śākhā*);
for at certain times and in certain places, there is the disappearance of specific Vedic branches (*śākhā-viśeṣa*).
