Furthermore, since these [Vedic branches] are set in motion by Vyāsa and others at certain times and in certain places, let it be that they possess the nature of having their root-branches destroyed.
And it was stated by the venerable Āpastamba: "The readings of those [branches] which have been lost are inferred from their usage."

The authority of the words of Manu and others is established by the Veda itself even without recourse to logic, through such passages as: "Whatever Manu said is medicine. Likewise, the authority of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is established by: "As they would conduct themselves there, so should you conduct yourselves here," and "Those good deeds which are ours..."
“They should be attended upon by you,” and so forth;
and the Smṛti also says: “The tradition and conduct of those who know that, as well as the practice of the virtuous,” and so on.
Anticipating the objection, "If the determination of Dharma can be accomplished by the Veda alone, what is the purpose of the *Dharmaśāstra*?
Marīci says: "The Vedic words are difficult to understand, and those [portions] which are scattered and supplementary (*khila*) are likewise obscure;
therefore, it is by those who know them that these have been established in the system of the *Smṛtis* with their meanings made clear."
Thus, even though the Dharmaśāstra exists, Devala demonstrates the dependence upon the Gṛhyasūtras: "Manu and others are proclaimed as the authors of the Dharmaśāstra;
the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras are the users of that [Dharmaśāstra] through their own mantras."
Thus, the determination of the meaning of the Veda depends upon the Dharmaśāstras, the Gṛhyasūtras, and so forth;
and in cases of conflict, the established rule regarding their relative strength and weakness applies accordingly.

However, regarding the *Bhagavad-dharma-śāstra* (the Pāñcarātra), even in the event of conflict with the Vedas (*śruti*) and other authorities, there is only an option (*vikalpa*), similar to the case of the taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; for it is established that this [Pāñcarātra] is free from the possibility of defects, just like the Veda, by virtue of its having as its object specific places, times, qualified persons, and circumstances.
And the learned have said thus, beginning with: "Because of the absence of an author and so forth in the Veda..."
Therefore, Sāṃkhya along with Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and in some places the Pañcarātra—this entire [system] is understood as authoritative from the fifth Veda alone.
Thus it is said.
And elsewhere: "In many Upaniṣads, the one whose banner is Tārkṣya (Viṣṇu) is proclaimed as a mass of qualities unassailed by defects;
even the Śruti does not admit an alternative to the Pañcarātras originating from him. This was well stated by the venerable Yāmunārya, the author of the Bhāṣya.
Thus,
this very point has been elaborated by the teacher Yāmunācārya in his *Āgamaprāmāṇya* through the refutation of all possible arguments of the opposing side.
In accordance with that very [view], the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have explained the *Pāñcarātra-adhikaraṇa*:
"This *tantra* has its root in the *Śruti*; it is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), like the *Kalpasūtras*.
Such statements, however, are to be understood as having their basis in the *Trayī* (the three Vedas) and their basis in the *Ekāyana-śruti*.

And one should not doubt its status as the Veda here: "This great [work], which is the root of the vast tree of the Veda, exists within the *vākas*, the *anuvākas*, the *niṣads*, and the *upaniṣads*."
"O Sage, the Ṛgveda and the others have become its trunks, and likewise they have become its branches," according to such statements;
and likewise, because the reading "This vow is very difficult to perform" is found in the recitation of the Ṛgveda, as shown by this corroboration.
Because even the *Nirukta* branch was included among the branches of the Veda during the period of Vyāsa’s distribution;

and because, in the *Sāttvata*, *Pauṣkara*, and other scriptures which constitute the essence of the Lord’s teachings, the authority of that [Ekāyana] Śruti is established in the injunctions for the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*) through such statements as: “With the supremely purifying mantras declared in the *Ekāyanīya* branch,” and so forth.

In this regard, the following passage uttered by the venerable Bhagavad-Yāmunamuni is recorded: "As for what was said— that 'the Brāhmaṇahood of the Bhāgavatas is lost because they practice other sacraments such as those beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with cremation'—
in that matter too, it is ignorance alone that is at fault,
and not the fault of your long-lived self."

Since these people, following their lineage, study the Vājasaneyi branch and perform the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* according to the path prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of Kātyāyana and others;
and since those who, from the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* onwards, perform the forty sacraments ordained in the *Ekāyana-śruti* without abandoning the duties of the triple Veda (*trayīdharma*)—

they too, by properly observing the dharma prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of their own branch, do not fall away from Brahminhood merely because they do not perform the rituals belonging to other branches.

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even others [belonging to different branches] would lose their Brahminhood due to the non-performance of rites prescribed by each other's branches;

for everywhere, conventional practices are observed as being strictly regulated by distinctions such as caste (*jāti*), Vedic school (*caraṇa*), lineage (*gotra*), and specific entitlement (*adhikāra*).
Even though a single rite is recognized across all branches, [the practice remains restricted].
Nevertheless, duties connected to mutually distinct qualifications are never combined;
for they are distinct from those qualified for rites such as the *aindrāgneya*, which are means for attaining the enjoyment of objects like heaven and sons as prescribed by the three Vedas.

Those Brāhmaṇas who, having been authorized for the performance of rituals— such as approaching the teacher (*abhigamana*), receiving instruction (*upādāna*), and sacrifice (*ijyā*)— which are prescribed by the *Upaniṣads* (the end of the triple Veda) and the *Ekāyana-śruti*, and which constitute the sole means for attaining the Lord, are seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*). Thus,
the non-performance of the rituals prescribed in each other’s recensional branches (*śākhā*) does not result in the loss of Brāhmaṇahood for either group.

"Just as the non-human (apauruṣeya) origin of the Ekāyana branch [of the Veda] has been explained, so too has the authority of the Kāśmīra Āgama been elaborated upon; therefore, it is not introduced here.

However, the clear perception of the connection of the Bhāgavatas under discussion with the Trayī—through the recitation of the Sāvitrī and other such practices—does not tolerate any doubt regarding their being *vrātyas* or the like on account of having abandoned that [Trayī]."
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Chapter 1, Section 45: And this Pañcarātra is fourfold— namely, the Āgama-siddhānta,
the Divya-siddhānta, and the Tantra-siddhānta.
In this regard, there is the internal doctrine (*antarasiddhānta*).
This fourfold expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) pertains to that portion which constitutes the root of the Veda;
for it is with reference to this intention that it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "This great [work] is the root of the vast tree of the Veda."
And so forth.
Furthermore, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and other attributes of these four have been shown by the Blessed One himself in the *Śrīpauṣkara* and other scriptures.

Moreover, whatever is to be said regarding those four—such as their commonality and uniqueness, their being subsumed under worship (*arcā*) or not being so subsumed, and so on—[is likewise established].

All of that has been established by us through a comprehensive examination in the *Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣāsiddhāntavyavasthā*; therefore, the details thereof should be investigated by those who are not alien to the protector of the Sāttvata dharma, and we shall not elaborate upon them here.
This being the case, some who are like the Bāhlīkas and stand outside the Āgamas take their rest in the authority of the venerable *Vaikhānasa* tradition.
In that regard, first of all, the Kalpasūtra is not a non-authoritative source, precisely because it is a Kalpasūtra like any other,
and because its author is universally recognized as a composer of Kalpasūtras.
Because it is not in contradiction with the Vedas; because all religious duties are prescribed by Vedic mantras alone;
and because even other Sūtras, in certain instances such as the characteristics of the construction of sacrificial altars (*kuṇḍa*), rely upon those [Vedic sources].

This is because it is conducive to the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), and because the teaching that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme goal is itself rooted in *sattva* and is thus the sole cause of its authoritative validity;
for it is said: "One should constantly remember Hari even before and after ritual acts;
one should meditate on the Lord Nārāyaṇa during rites such as bathing."
Since Śaunaka and others have likewise prescribed this through such passages as these,
and since there is no possibility of corruption because the text has been studied by the Vaikhānasas through an unbroken lineage of transmission;
let that be as it may.
If it is asked what the criterion for determining "this is that" is,
it is the non-perception of anything else and the perception of that very thing;
otherwise, there would result a pervasive doubt regarding the Vedas, Smṛtis, and so forth, in every instance.
Let it be that this alone is the authority; nevertheless, how can the four [sages] beginning with Bhārgava possess authority?
If it is argued thus, we say no, because the same response has already been given;
for the reasons such as being composed by great sages and not contradicting the Vedas apply equally [to both systems].
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the Pañcarātra, we say no.
Because that [distinction] does not exist in reality,
for even the distinction between duties and actions is justified solely by virtue of being directed toward specific qualified persons,
just as in the case of the different ritual procedures of the Kalpasūtras.

In the *Āśvamedhika* [Parvan] of the *Śrīvaiṣṇava-dharmaśāstra*, both [the Āgama and Tantrāntara systems] are accepted as having equal authority, just as the *Pañcarātra* is divided into four internal categories such as Kriyā and so forth.
The mutual authority of both is indicated in passages such as: "The Tantra of Viṣṇu is declared to be twofold."

As for the mutually contradictory statements, they were either uttered by those who, desiring to consume sugarcane, were unable to endure [the opponent's views], or they are merely figurative praises intended to extol their own scriptures; thus, there is no contradiction therein.
Nyāyapañcāśikā, Chapter 46: Now, it may be objected that the Bhārgava and other such texts are not indeed Kalpasūtras,
because they are not accepted as such,
because they are not well-known, and because they are illogical.

Nor are they other Smṛtis, because they are not recited among the works of Manu and others, and because they lack the same established authority; nor are they independent systems (tantra), since they are never seen mentioned alongside Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the like.
And because they follow the Vaikhānasa tradition,
by adopting which of these categories is their authority asserted?
Like those of Manu, Atri, Bhārgava, and others, and like the Nāradīya and other such works, their authority is established precisely as Dharmaśāstras.
For authoritative persons accept that the enumeration of eighteen and so forth is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
If it is argued that there is no detailed elaboration (*prapañcana*) regarding festivals for the gods and so on in other Smṛtis,
let there be no such elaboration.
The true nature [of these texts] has indeed been established for those devoted to their detailed exposition;
nevertheless, one might argue that because there is ultimately a universal disparity among individual souls, these [texts] are intended only for those of inferior qualification.
This is not so, because it is stated that among both these and others, the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is the sole primary qualification.
And because they are perceived as such.
If it is asked, "How can they possess Brahminhood?",
let that evil be stilled.
We shall cover our ears;
nevertheless, it must be said:

for here are seen these Brāhmaṇas, who study the Veda through a continuous lineage, who possess all the Vedic sacraments prescribed in the Vaikhānasa Sūtras, who are diligent in the duties and rituals of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), and who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed Lord.
Surely it is only because of their being devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavata*)—and solely on that account of their Brahminhood—that this "donkey of a Brahmin" wanders about in confusion;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the *Vaikhānasa-kalpa* would lack authority due to its having no qualified practitioners.
Let its authority be granted.
And let there be those authorized for it in another place or at another time; but if you ask, "Who are these [authorities]?"—
it can be said that this is equally possible even in another place and so forth.
Or why should it not be the opposite?
And this being the case, what confidence can there be even in other sūtras and such?
If it is argued that [the status of the Vaikhānasas] is a subject of doubt due to both the statement regarding their low birth and the existence of disputes, [we reply:]...

Because there is no such statement in the texts of authoritative tradition (*āpta-grantha*); because even if such a statement existed, there would be no evidence for their being of an inferior caste (*nikṛṣṭa-jāti*);
and because it is equally consistent with the application of designations such as "Sātvata" and so forth, as stated in the *Āgama-prāmāṇya*.
For it is not the case that there is no word with multiple meanings, nor does the identity of a word entail the identity of its meaning, nor does a difference in words entail a difference in meaning.
Otherwise, [the matter] would have dissolved even with the third stage of life (*tṛtīyāśrama*);
for a dispute—which depends merely upon the movement of the tongue of someone like you—could easily be raised even regarding the *Sūtras*, the *Gotra*, and so forth.
If you say that [such a dispute] does not exist prior to this, we reply: no.
For this dispute also cannot be beginningless,
because it did not exist prior to that [first moment];
likewise, since there is no distinction in the nature of a dispute whether it belongs to you or will belong to you in the future, it would follow that they would lack confidence after that point.
If you say, "We have no doubt regarding those [beings]," then do we have any [doubt] regarding these?
Where, then, is there another inferior caste?
What has been entrusted to us that we must display?
For it is not possible for us to see infinite lands.
Furthermore, annihilation is possible now, just as in the case of the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Māhiṣyas, and so forth.
If it is argued that their entry here is possible merely because some among them share the same name, we say no.
Because some kind of doubt is easily found everywhere;
furthermore, there is a similarity between being a member of a caste and being a monk, and so forth, even elsewhere.
And he who is thus tormented by excessive suspicion—
But since he might, by failing to ascertain the conduct of his own parents, come to doubt even his own status as a brahmin in a manner that is not appropriate, the Lokāyata position is won.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "The ignorant one, the faithless one, and the doubting soul perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world nor the next, nor is there happiness."
Thus,
it is established that the Smṛti traditions of the Vaikhānasas and others, which pertain to specific qualifications and are not in conflict with the Vedas, are authoritative.
As for the enumeration of eighteen and so forth found in the Dharmaśāstras and other texts, [it is merely illustrative].
It does not aim to exclude a greater number [of authorities],
because others as well— such as those accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*)— are indistinguishable [in their authority],
and because [the Veda] is dependent [on them] through the observation of unmentioned portions and so forth.
Thus, it is established that the Veda, together with its ancillaries, is a valid means of knowledge.
“Chandas is the feet, Śabdaśāstra is the mouth, Kalpa is the hands, and Jyotiṣa is the eyes;
Śikṣā is the nose and Nirukta is said to be the ears—these six are declared to be the limbs (aṅgas) of the Veda.”

"Thus, the Mīmāṃsā consisting of twenty chapters—beginning with 'Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma' (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.1) and ending with 'Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement' (Brahma Sūtra 4.4.22)—has as its subject matter the determination of the true meaning of the Vedas along with their ancillaries.

And therein, this [work] concerning the Self (Śārīraka) is joined with Jaimini’s sixteen-chapter [work], which establishes the unity of the scripture. This is the passage from the Vṛtti cited in the Bhāṣya.
In the *Tattvaratnākara*, however, it is stated as follows: "That [scripture] emerged in three ways concerning the scope of karma, the deities, and Brahman, according to the author of the Sūtras:
from the sage Jaimini, from Kāśakṛtsna, and from Bādarāyaṇa, respectively."

Thus, these two statements—regarding the Devatākāṇḍa being the work of Jaimini and that of Kāśakṛtsna respectively—are to be understood as having the same meaning, intended with reference to its dependence [on the ritual section] and so forth.

In that regard, they have summarized the subject matter of the Karmakāṇḍa as follows: "The knowledge of Dharma [is established] through the distinctions of the means of knowledge, the subsidiaries, the application, the sequence, and the agent."
"Along with the specific extensions, the obstructions, and the application of the tantras."

Thus: "The investigation of the meaning of the Veda through reasoning was first completed; that [investigation] concerned ritual action and its deities. Now, therefore, in the portion concerning the embodied self (Śārīraka), there is the investigation of Brahman, which yields infinite fruit.

In that [work], in the first chapter, there are two topics each consisting of a pair: the concordance of the Upaniṣads with the Supreme [Brahman] itself and their lack of contradiction [therewith]; and the means to liberation and liberation itself, the latter being the object and the former the subject, the latter being established and the former to be accomplished."

In that [work], first are considered the words for the Self (ātman), the vital breath (prāṇa), and so forth—which are extremely hidden, obscure, or clear; then, by means of recollection and other methods, the unimpaired cognition of the effect-ness of the sense organs and so on;

then, in the third [section], defects and non-defects regarding the lower and higher goals; then, devotion, the limbs [of yoga], and finally, in the last [section], meditation on the power of the performance of worship, the sequence [of stages], the path, and the fruits.
"Prior to inquiry itself, the study [of the Veda] has already been accomplished by the injunction;
therefore, inquiry for one who has not studied the Veda is contradicted by the scriptures."
The sequence of the twenty characteristics is not based on scriptural injunction (vaidha), but rather is logical (yauktika);
therefore, in the case of considering them out of order, impropriety is established.

Nyāyapañcāśikā, verse 48: Thus, for one who has become well-established in the entire meaning of the scriptures through hearing and reflection upon the twenty characteristics, the practice enjoined as the means to liberation is *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), and not merely the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-jñāna*), because the latter is already established through hearing and so forth, which occur by the force of natural inclination (*rāga*).
For this very reason, the general terms such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so on find their ultimate application in that specific [contemplation].
Nor should it be argued that practices such as *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) are not prohibited, but rather that being chosen [by God] alone is enjoined;
for the state of being the object of a choice made by another independent agent is not something dependent on the person and is therefore not subject to injunction.
Therefore, by that very cause—namely, its nature as joy—it is meditation itself that is distinguished;
this being so, there is no contradiction with the Smṛti statement, "But by unswerving devotion.
And that very meditation, consisting of joy, is samādhi due to the specific context.
Furthermore, the eight-limbed [path] is taught in the treatises,
and Patañjali’s authority is valid to that extent;
moreover, the practice of the traditional scriptures (āgama) should be followed with moderation until the fruit is attained.
And they remember: "One should practice yoga through Vedic study; one should enter into Vedic study through yoga.
Through the perfection of both Vedic study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed."
Thus it is said;
furthermore, it is heard: "The wise person, devoted to knowledge and realization, having mastered the text, should discard the book entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw."
Thus, that [statement] intends the relinquishing of the treasury;

for a person who possesses the perfection of intelligence—accomplished through the accumulation of refined mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) characterized by respect and skill—the treasury has nothing further to achieve.
Furthermore, he is specifically distinguished as "intelligent" (*medhāvī*).
The lexicographers state: "Dhī is wisdom endowed with retention (dhāraṇā).
And we recite: "May wisdom and intelligence enter me together for the attainment of what has been and what is to be.
Or rather, this [verse] refers to a person whose yoga is nearly liberated and completely perfected.
For at that time, there is nothing for him to be known through scripture, because he has directly realized the meaning of all principles.
As it is said in the Smṛti: "Knowledge derived from scripture involves much affliction and is a cause of the mind's fluctuation."
Having understood Hari through this instruction, one should desist from all ritual actions.
Thus, this [teaching] is to be accepted by those who possess intense spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and those who are indolent yet faithful;
or else, it is for the purpose of abandoning false treatises that cause the mind to waver.
In that case, the qualification [of the teaching] is fruitful.

For even an excessive zeal for the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) other than the Dharma is rejected for one who seeks liberation: “Liberation is not for one who delights in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), nor for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings;
not for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one who takes pleasure in winning over the minds of worldly people.”
Thus, for those who desire to understand the reality of objects of knowledge through verbal testimony, this [scripture] is the essence among the means of valid cognition;
for in its absence, it would follow that human beings are equal to beasts.
May that Nārāyaṇa, whose command resides like a female dove upon the roof-peak of the mansion of the Vedas, who holds Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods under the sway of his playful brow,
and who, assuming universal forms, eternally spreads his names everywhere as of old— he, the ultimate goal of all speech, may he shine forth before us.

Thus ends the second Āhnika in the Śabdādhyāya of the Nyāyapariśuddhi, a work of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrīmad Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all systems of thought;
and with it, the third Adhyāya is completed.
